segments.note: ātmavastu is the thing taken as self, not the self: the skandhas bring to light five bases on which the idea of a self rests.
segments.concepts: *ātmavastu* — the „basis of self“: what the notion of a self is projected onto; the AS derives the number of the skandhas from the five ways such a basis appears.

grammar: One question and its answer, the catechism form of the AS.  The question (22) is a nominal sentence with an understood copula: kasmāt pañcaiva skandhāḥ.  The answer (23–28) has no finite verb: six accusatives in -udbhāvanatām, each governed by the gerund upādāya used as a postposition („on account of“).  23 states the principle — the self-basis appears in five modes —, 24–28 list the five, each a compound ending in -ātmavastūdbhāvanatām.
translation: Why are there just five aggregates (skandha)? — On account of their bringing to light (udbhāvanatā) the basis of self (ātmavastu) in five modes: the self-basis that is the body together with its possessions (saparigraha-deha), the self-basis that is experience (upabhoga), the self-basis that is conventional expression (vyavahāra), the self-basis that is the forming of merit and demerit (dharmādharmābhisaṃskāra), and the self-basis that is the support of these (tadāśraya).
comparison: Rahula/Boin-Webb reduce ātmavastu to „self“ and turn the forming of merit and demerit into „the agent“; DharmaMitra keeps the basis („objective basis“, with an added „objective“) and stays close to udbhāvanatā („manifest“).  Neither reflects the Tibetan's „stating“ (brjod pa).
